Chapter 8: Troubleshooting Common Obstacles
Even when you’re putting in steady effort, it’s totally normal to hit some bumps along the road as you work on changing your self-talk. These obstacles pop up for just about everyone—but the good news is, there are practical ways to move through them.
Let’s start with doubt and skepticism. Have you ever tried saying something positive to yourself, only for your mind to push back and say, “Come on, that’s not true”? That’s a really common reaction, especially if you’ve been carrying old beliefs for a long time. The trick here is to start with baby steps. Instead of jumping straight to “I am amazing,” try something that feels honest, like, “I’m open to learning,” or, “I’m making progress.” As you notice even tiny wins, your mind gets more comfortable with the bigger, more powerful affirmations down the line.
Now, about inconsistency. Life gets busy, doesn’t it? It’s easy to forget to practice self-talk when you’re juggling a million things. One helpful strategy is to link your new habit to something you already do every day—like brushing your teeth, commuting to work, or preparing a meal. Just a moment or two each day really does add up. And if you skip a day? No big deal. Just start again, and leave the guilt behind.
What about emotional triggers? Sometimes, strong feelings like anger, fear, or sadness can drag you right back into old patterns. When this happens, try pausing for a second and just acknowledging what you’re feeling. Then, use self-talk to comfort yourself—maybe something like, “It’s okay to feel this way. I can handle this.” With practice, this helps break the automatic link between tough emotions and negative self-talk.
You might also face moments where it feels like you’re not making progress. Change can be slow, especially when old habits are stubborn. Here’s the thing—progress isn’t always a straight line. Celebrate those small wins, and if you hit a setback, look at it as a chance to learn. If you feel stuck, consider tweaking your self-talk statements or reaching out for support. Sometimes a little encouragement from someone else makes all the difference.
Finally, let’s talk about social and environmental influences. The people and places around us can sometimes reinforce the old stories we tell ourselves. If you can, spend more time with folks who genuinely support your growth. Try to limit time around negative influences, and remind yourself, “I choose what I believe about myself.” That mindset can be a real anchor.
By expecting these obstacles and knowing how to handle them, you’ll stay on track and keep building a more supportive conversation with yourself. Remember, every step counts.
